extracted.intended_audience: regulated businesses, legal counsel, policy stakeholders, and participants in FTC rulemaking/notice-and-comment on non-compete regulation
extracted.subtask_description: Legal and administrative standards the Federal Trade Commission invokes to justify promulgating a rule that defines certain non-compete clauses as unfair methods of competition, including statutory authority, substantive legal tests, procedural obligations, and illustrative precedents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commission rulemaking authority under section 6(g)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission may promulgate rules under section 6(g) of the FTC Act to define unfair methods of competition; the Commission concludes that its rulemaking authority under section 6(g) (and use of that power to define non-competes) does not implicate the major questions doctrine and Congress has provided express statutory authority for both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Part II.B for history of using section 6(g); references W. Va. v. EPA and other cases addressing major questions; notes commenters' challenges and the Commission's conclusion that section 6(g) provides express authority to promulgate substantive rules on unfair methods of competition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 5 substantive reach (unfair methods of competition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 5 reaches a broad array of anticompetitive conduct and permits the Commission to define and prohibit 'unfair methods of competition' without being limited to traditional antitrust proof frameworks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Supreme Court and appellate cases (e.g., FTC v. Texaco, Brown Shoe) and the FTC Policy Statement describing principles of general applicability; explains that section 5 can be elaborated through rulemaking or case-by-case adjudication.

rubrics_metrics.name: No requirement for market-definition or proof of market power under section 5
rubrics_metrics.description: Finding an unfair method of competition under section 5 does not require market definition or proof of market power; the inquiry into commercial setting need not entail a full-scale economic market analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supported by cases (e.g., Motion Picture Advert. Serv., Atl. Refin. Co., Texaco) and FTC Policy Statement; the Commission may rely on reasonable tendency to injure competition rather than detailed market-power proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of 'reasonable tendency' standard (no showing of actual harm necessary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practices may be unlawful under section 5 based on their reasonable tendency to injure or obstruct competition; evidence of actual past harm is not required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Union Circulation Co., Ethyl, In re Coca-Cola Co.; courts have upheld findings based on tendency rather than demonstrated actual harm to competition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categories of conduct that can be unfair methods of competition
rubrics_metrics.description: Unfair methods of competition include practices that are 'collusive, coercive, predatory, restrictive or deceitful' as well as 'exclusionary'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drawn from case law (Ethyl, Sperry & Hutchinson) and the FTC Policy Statement; examples in the text include price-fixing, exclusive dealing, monopoly maintenance, false advertising, and agreements restricting employment.

rubrics_metrics.name: No blanket application of the rule of reason to section 5
rubrics_metrics.description: The text and precedent do not support applying the antitrust 'rule of reason' as the required framework to determine whether conduct violates section 5 as an unfair method of competition in this rulemaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explained in Parts II.A, II.B, II.C, II.F; cites Supreme Court and circuit precedent and notes commenters' suggestions to apply rule of reason but rejects them based on statutory text, case law, and legislative history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commission's adjudicatory power complements rulemaking power
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission may address unfair methods of competition either through general rulemaking or through case-by-case adjudication; both forms of action are permissible and necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Nat'l Petroleum Refiners Ass'n v. FTC and Chenery principles; agency must be able to act by general rule or individual order depending on circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural obligations under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Agency rulemaking must comply with APA notice-and-comment requirements (e.g., publish notice of a proposed rule, solicit and consider public comments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites 5 U.S.C. 553 and Elec. Priv. Info. Ctr. v. DHS; the Commission notes commenters' claims that the NPRM failed to consider key aspects and states that it has addressed those concerns in other parts of the statement of basis and purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to consider alternatives, reliance interests, and State policy concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: In responding to comments, the Commission must consider arguments that it failed to consider key aspects of the rulemaking, including less restrictive alternatives, State policy interactions, and reliance interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paragraph summarizes types of commenter objections (failure of reasoned decision-making, not considering less restrictive alternatives, State policy, reliance interests) and notes the Commission's responses elsewhere in the document.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commission will not necessarily accept industry justifications in section 5 analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: For certain anticompetitive practices, courts and the Commission have not accepted proffered justifications as a defense to unlawful conduct under section 5 or related antitrust precedent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Atlantic Refin., Texaco, Balfour, and other cases where claimed efficiencies or benefits to firms did not excuse otherwise illegal practices; the Commission warns it will similarly not accept certain justifications pursued through section 5.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevalence and far-reaching consequences as a factor in public-interest assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: A practice that is widespread and far-reaching in its consequences can be of public concern and relevant to the Commission's assessment under the statute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites R.F. Keppel & Bro. and Texaco: 'A practice so widespread and so far reaching in its consequences is of public concern if in other respects within the purview of the statute.' The Commission may consider prevalence as part of its analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: FTC jurisdictional scope (entities covered)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission analyzes coverage focusing on 'corporations' and may exercise jurisdiction over entities claiming nonprofit tax-exempt status when pecuniary benefits to for-profit actors are present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites 15 U.S.C. 44 and various FTC orders and decisions addressing nonprofits and entities providing pecuniary benefit; notes the Commission cannot precisely predict how many nonprofits may be reached but finds benefits justify the rule's implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commission's interpretive primacy and interaction with other agencies' enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpretive authority over the FTC Act rests with the Commission; whether other agencies (e.g., FDIC) enforce or apply the rule to entities under their jurisdiction is a separate question for those agencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explained through discussion of commenters' concerns about FDIC enforcement of banks and general principle that the FTC interprets the Act while other agencies may have enforcement roles within their jurisdictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Labor-mobility and employment restraints as potential unfair methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Agreements among competitors that restrict hiring or employment relationships (e.g., 'no-poach' or agreements not to employ each other's employees) can restrict freedom to enter employment relationships and may impair competition in the supply of services or labor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supported by Nichols v. Spencer Intern. Press and Union Circulation Co.; examples and prior Commission orders show restraint on labor mobility may be treated as an unfair method of competition under section 5.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of historical precedents and enforcement examples to inform rulemaking
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission relies on prior orders, consent decrees, enforcement actions, roundtables, and industry investigations as evidence and expertise when developing rules (including examples where parties agreed to cease enforcing non-competes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text cites recent investigations, consent orders, and cases (e.g., Impax Labs., Inc.) and references Parts I.B and other sections documenting Commission experience and expertise with non-competes.
